doc.title: Michael White interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 10, 2025

chapter: Dance music, function and ensemble playing
title: Space and Kid Thomas Valentine
summary: White praises the importance of rests and recalls Kid Thomas Valentine's minimalist, spacious style.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: And don’t forget about the rests.

Yes. Space is very important as well. Because the music has to breathe. Even if the rhythm plays and there’s nothing quite going on right there, if it’s breathing in part of the rhythm it can be great. One of the interesting players I played with was Kid Thomas Valentine, who was a trumpet player. He was born in 1896, before Louis Armstrong. And he had his own kind of style, big beautiful, expressive tone. But he was what I would call a minimalist. He reminded me of middle-period Miles Davis in that sense in that he would leave a lot of spaces. He played a basic melody his own way, his own phrasing, his own tone. But he would leave spaces and it was good to do a response to or play rhythms or obbligato with. But also then it would still have spaces. And somehow that made the music flow a certain kind of way. It was great you know, because you just hear the rhythm of the banjo and the bass and the drum in between all that, it was beautiful.
